text.4: Chapter 1 ClassMate's First Day. The buzz started before the first bell even rang. "Did you hear? It goes live today!" Zara said, juggling her backpack and her tablet. "Maybe it'll do my math homework," joked Niko, earning a laugh from the row behind him. "I've used AI before," said Mia. "My dad's car can stop itself if someone walks in front of it." Zara nodded. "Our TV app even guesses what shows I'll like next. It's usually right!" "Good morning, everyone," Ms. Vega said with a smile.
text.5: "Sounds like you already know a little about artificial intelligence. AI is part of lots of things we use every day. Like games, maps, even medical robots and traffic lights." "Yep," interjected Niko, "I love how my game system gets harder as it learns how I play." "That's a great example," Ms. Vega continued, "Our district's new AI helper, called ClassMate, is designed to make school tasks easier. Starting today, you'll be able to use it on your tablets, in the library, even in the cafeteria. It offers tools that can support our learning, like recommending books, helping us write, or turning speech into text. Let's try one out together." The ClassMate logo, a friendly blue swirl, flashed onto the board.
text.6: AI stands for artificial intelligence: computer programs that learn from data to make predictions or suggestions. "Let's start with the speech-to-text tool. Who'd like to volunteer?" James raised his hand first. "Hi, ClassMate. Please write: Today is Tuesday and I love science class." "Today is Tuesday and I love science class." "Nice! Who's next?" Malik spoke up. "Hi, ClassMate. My name is Malik, and my favorite subject is history." "Hi, ClassMate. My name is Mallet, and my favorite sub sandwich is mystery." "Hmm..."
text.7: "It looks like ClassMate didn't hear that correctly. It's still learning to understand different voices and accents." "It's not you. Sometimes AI just messes up." How do you think Malik felt when ClassMate got his name wrong? Have you ever had technology misunderstand you?
text.8: At lunch, ClassMate was everywhere! Screens at the checkout line blinked with suggestions. "Good afternoon, Mia!" read the screen. "You might like today's chicken nuggets with honey mustard." Mia groaned. "I'm a vegetarian!" The cafeteria attendant shrugged, "I guess it doesn't know that yet."
text.9: Niko's turn came next. "Recommended for you: Peanut butter sandwich," said the voice. He stepped back quickly. "Uh, no thanks — I'm allergic to peanuts!" A teacher rushed over to double-check his tray. Nothing dangerous had happened, but the line of students backed up behind Niko craned their heads, whispering. "So it just gives random food suggestions?" Zara asked, once they all sat down. "Maybe," said Mia. "Or maybe it's guessing based on what we picked before." "Yeah," said Niko. "Probably no one told it about our allergies." They all looked at the screen. It still glowed with friendly blue light, ready to assist the next student in line.
text.10: That afternoon, the class walked to the library for independent reading. "ClassMate can help you find your next great book!" said Mr. Taylor, the librarian. "Just type or say the kinds of books you like." Zara typed: I love mysteries. ClassMate responded immediately: You might like Space Explorers: Book 4! She blinked. "That's not a mystery. I read that last year." Niko laughed. "It probably thinks you still love space!" Mia tried next. "I like stories about friendship," she said aloud. ClassMate replied: Recommended: The Art of Drawing Faces. "That's not about friendship," Mia sighed.
text.11: Data: Information we collect to help us learn or make decisions. It can be numbers, words, pictures, videos, or sounds. Data works best when it helps us answer a question or reach a goal. So it's kind of like guessing. Kind of. And sometimes it guesses wrong. Ai systems make predictions based on data. If the data is old or incomplete, The predictions might not match what'S really happening. • Have you ever had someone make an assumption about you based on old information? How did it feel? • What could ClassMate learn if it had newer or more complete data about the students' interests? • What would be a fair way for an AI system to update its data?
text.12: Back in class, Ms. Vega invited everyone to share their experiences. "So," she asked, "how did ClassMate do today?" "Pretty good," Hannah said. "I liked the honey mustard sauce it recommended to go with my chicken nuggets." "Pretty bad," Niko said. "It tried to feed me peanuts." "It called me 'Mallet,'" said Malik quietly, but everyone heard. "It kept recommending the same old books I've already read," added Zara. So, it worked better for some of you than others. Why do you think that is? A few hands went up. "Maybe it didn't have enough examples?" Mia suggested. "Or it practiced on voices that sound different from mine," said Malik. "Or maybe it hasn't learned what we like yet," added James. Ms. Vega wrote their ideas on the board: Not enough examples. Different voices. Old information.
text.13: "Those are really smart guesses," she said. "Here's something important to remember: AI isn't magic. It doesn't just know things. It learns from data that people give it." Zara frowned. "So people teach it, like teachers teach us?" "Exactly," said Ms. Vega. "Programmers, librarians, and testers decide what information it sees, what examples it practices on, and how it makes decisions. That means their choices can change how well it works, and who it works for." The class grew quiet for a moment. Malik raised his hand. "So if they only give it certain kinds of voices or names, it might get others wrong?" "Yes," said Ms. Vega. "That's why it's so important that the people who build AI think about everyone when they design it." She paused and looked around the room. "So, who really has the power when we use AI?" The people who build it. And the people who decide what it learns from. What kinds of jobs do you think help build or improve AI systems? • Why is it important for people in those jobs to come from different backgrounds and experiences? • How could that help make AI fair?
text.14: The bell for dismissal was only ten minutes away, but nobody was packing up yet. Ms. Vega leaned against her desk, marker in hand. "So," she said, "if we were the team in charge of improving ClassMate, what would we do differently?" Hands shot up. "Give it more examples," said Mia. "Like, if it keeps getting someone's name wrong, add more recordings of how people actually say it." "Yeah," said Malik. "And make sure it hears voices from lots of different people, not just the same ones." "Or update it more often," Niko added. "If it only knows what we liked to read last year, no wonder it's confused." "These are great ideas," said Ms. Vega, jotting on the board.
text.15: Zara leaned forward. "What about adding a way for us to tell it when it's wrong? Like a little button that says, 'That's not right'. Then it could learn from that." Ms. Vega smiled. "Excellent idea! That's called giving feedback, something AI systems really need." The list on the board grew longer: More examples. Diverse voices. Updated information. Feedback from users. People checking the results. Ms. Vega capped her marker. "You know what's interesting? Every idea you just shared involves people. Even when we use AI, humans are still the ones who make it work fairly and safely."
text.16: The bell rang, and everyone began gathering their things. As Zara zipped her backpack, she looked back at the smartboard. The ClassMate logo glowed faintly on the corner of the screen. "Hey, Ms. Vega?" Zara said "Maybe we should give ClassMate more examples of what we actually like for lunch, or books, or whatever. That might help it." Ms. Vega nodded. "I think that's a great place to start." James elbowed Malik. "I guess sometimes even the helper needs some help." They laughed as they shuffled toward the door. Just before leaving, Zara glanced once more at the board. AI can be really good at things, but people have to make sure it works for everyone.
text.17: LET'S see what you learned! Chapter 1 Activities
text.18: Chapter 1 Activities. Instructions: ClassMate needs more information about books in the library so that it can make better recommendations for students. Give ClassMate more information by checking the correct description for each book. Some books may have more than one check. Books: Magic Tree House. Diary of a Wimpy Kid. Owl Diaries. The Friendship Garden. Space Explorers. Your book choice. Your book choice. Description choices for each book: Adventure. Animals. Funny. Science. Friendship.
text.19: THINK ABOUT IT: How will giving ClassMate more examples help it make better suggestions for everyone? Why does ClassMate need many examples to recommend books that each student will like?
text.20: Chapter 2 The Sensing Lab. The next day, Ms. Vega wrote three big words on the board: The Sensing Lab "This morning," she announced, "ClassMate made another mistake, and our mission is to figure out why." "Of course it did," James said, exasperated. Zara leaned forward with interest. "What kind of mistake?" Ms. Vega smiled. "You'll see. Before we get into it, we need to understand how ClassMate senses things in the first place." Niko scratched his head. "Senses? Like smell and taste?" "Well, yes," said Ms. Vega, "Those are how we sense things. As you know, humans have five main senses. Computers have sensors too, but they're not the same as our human senses. Let's see how they compare." She directed the students' attention down to their table.
text.21: On each table sat a tray with four items: a lemon, a piece of sandpaper, a small magnet, and a metal spoon. "Start simple," said Ms. Vega. "Describe each object using your senses. Remember, your five senses are seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and feeling." Mia picked up the lemon. "It looks yellow and feels bumpy. If I cut it open, I know it tastes sour." Niko rubbed the sandpaper. "Feels rough! Like it could scrape paint right off the wall." Zara held up the magnet. "It's smooth and kind of cold. But... how do we sense magnetism?" Human senses: how we use our eyes to see, ears to hear, nose to smell, skin to feel, and tongue to taste to gather information Sensor: a device that collects information from the world, like a camera, microphone, or temperature reader Computer sensing: how machines detect things such as light, sound, heat, magnetism, or movement
text.22: "Good question," said Ms. Vega, smiling. "Humans can't feel that force with our senses-but computers with special sensors can." Ms. Vega held up her tablet. "Now, let's see what ClassMate senses." Ms. Vega opened the ClassMate Object Viewer tool and pointed the tablet's camera toward the tray. On the board, the live image appeared with labels that popped up as ClassMate tried to identify each item. ClassMate's text appeared instantly on the smartboard: Lemon: yellow, oval Sandpaper: brown, rectangle Magnet: silver, disc Malik scoffed. "That's it? It doesn't recognize that the lemon is a fruit?"
text.23: "Well, no. Not unless it was trained to recognize certain types of fruit. Thinking about it... computers can't smell or touch. They only record what their sensors can measure," said Ms. Vega. "To ClassMate, the lemon is just a shape and a color." "But let's try something humans can't sense as easily." Ms. Vega pulled a small plug-in camera from the supply bin and attached it to her tablet. "This special thermal camera works like a pair of superpower goggles to help ClassMate 'see' heat," she explained, "like some snakes, bugs, and fish! Even though we can't see heat with human eyes, the camera can. On the screen, bright colors (like red and yellow) mean something is hot, and dark colors (like blue and purple) mean something is cold." She aimed it toward the class. On the smart board, their warm faces glowed orange and red against a cool blue and purple background.
text.24: "Whoa!" said Niko. "It looks like we're on fire!" "Not fire," Ms. Vega corrected. "Just warm. Computers can sense heat energy even when our eyes can't." She pointed toward the window. "See that red patch? That's sunlight warming the glass. ClassMate can detect the temperature difference." Mia waved her hand in front of her face. "That's wild. It's like it has super-vision." "Kind of," said Ms. Vega. "Computers can sense things we can't, but that doesn't mean they understand them." Mia waved her arms even bigger, watching her image on the screen. "So like, it can tell we're warm, but not that we're people?"
text.25: "That's right," said Ms. Vega. "It just sees patterns of heat. To understand what those patterns mean, it needs humans to help interpret them." Ms. Vega unplugged the camera and opened a new tool on her tablet. A flat green line appeared on the smartboard. "Now let's look at how computers sense sound," she said. "When we speak or make noise, the microphone senses vibrations in the air and turns them into data." She clapped once. A tall spike jumped across the screen. "Cool!" said Zara. "It drew your clap." "It did," said Ms. Vega. "That's the sound wave. Louder sounds make taller spikes and quieter sounds make shorter ones." Niko drummed his pencil on the desk. The line rippled in a quick pattern. "It even shows rhythm!" he said.
text.26: "It does," Ms. Vega agreed. "A computer can measure how sound moves, but it doesn't hear it the way we do. The computer doesn't hear music or voices like we do. It doesn't know if a song is pretty or who is talking. Instead, it measures how loud the sound is and how high or low the notes of a song are." She switched to another tab labeled Speech-to-Text Demo. "We used this yesterday, but today we'll look at it differently. AI doesn't just detect sound; it can use data to guess what the sound means." "But it doesn't always get it right," Malik grumbled. "That's true, Malik. Tools like this one try to perceive what sounds mean," she explained, "But it can't hear and think like we do." She nodded to Mia. "Want to try?" Mia called out "ClassMate, write: The pencil is on the desk." "The pickle is on the desk."
text.27: The class burst out laughing. Mia groaned but smiled. "Close enough, I guess." Ms. Vega chuckled. "It's hearing the same sounds we do–it just hasn't learned the difference between pen-cil and pickle. Computers need lots of examples to make accurate guesses and those examples come from humans. Every time we use a speech-to-text tool like this, our words help train the system." Malik's eyes widened and his hand shot up. "So we're the ones who are teaching it right now?" "Exactly, Malik," said Ms. Vega. "Your words and actions today will train how the AI works tomorrow." • Why did ClassMate mistake "pencil" for "pickle?" • What kind of examples would help ClassMate learn to tell them apart?
text.28: After the laughter faded, Ms. Vega looked around the room. "So what did we notice today?" Computers can sense some things we can't. Like heat. And they can't sense some things we can. Like taste. And sometimes they get it half right, like calling a pencil a pickle. Right, computers and humans both collect information from the world, but in very different ways. Humans use memory, emotions, and experience to make sense of what we notice. Computers can only use the data we give them.
text.29: She turned to the smartboard and drew two columns. "Let's make a list together." What they do. Human senses. Sight: detect or sense colors, shapes, and textures. Hearing: detect or sense sound. Touch: detect or sense texture, pressure. Smell: detect or sense scents. Taste: detect or sense flavors. Computer sensors. Camera: detects light, color, patterns. Microphone: detects sound, vibrations. Distance or pressure sensor: detects distance, surface touch. Thermometer: detects air temperature. Smoke detector: detects smoke and gasses in the air. She stepped back so everyone could see the chart. "Both columns describe ways of noticing the world," she said. "But what makes them different?" "They don't mean the same things to the computer," said Malik. "It doesn't know what it's sensing. Just that there's a change." "Yes," said Ms. Vega. "Computers sense information, but they don't understand it until a human helps organize it. It's like if a computer could find every single blue LEGO in a giant bin, but it would still need you to show it how to build a house." She pointed to the camera icon on her tablet. "Tomorrow, we'll look at how computers do that. They take all the things they sense and organize them into representations-like maps, charts, or tables-to make sense of the world."
text.30: Zara tilted her head. "So that's kind of like what we do in science, when we make diagrams?" "Great connection," said Ms. Vega. "Humans and computers both use patterns to explain what they notice. That's how we move from sensing to understanding." As the students began lining up for music class, they were still chatting about the glowing heat maps; others kept joking about "pickle pencils." Mia grinned at James, "Gosh, I can't wait to see what ClassMate does next." We better teach it how to tell a pickle from a pencil, or things could get messy.
text.32: Chapter 2 Activities. Activity 1. How AI senses human actions. Directions: Read each human action in the table. For each row, choose which sensor the AI would use and put a checkmark in that box. Human action. How AI senses it. Speak to a smart assistant: camera, microphone, or keyboard. Type in a chatbot: camera, microphone, or keyboard. Wave to start a game: motion sensor, temperature probe, or speaker. Show an image to search: microphone, camera, or motion sensor. Discussion questions. Why do you think AI sometimes makes mistakes when it hears, sees, or watches something? Why do you think AI sometimes makes mistakes when it processes sounds, pictures, or videos?
text.33: Activity 2. Debug the AI. What went wrong? Directions: Read each situation. Fill in the table to explain how the person interacted with the AI, which sensor it used, and how we could improve the AI. Table columns. Situation. How did the person interact with the AI? Circle your answer: voice, text, picture, or movement. Which sensor did the AI use? Circle your answer: microphone, keyboard, camera, or motion sensor. What did the AI probably sense? Data. How could we help the AI improve? Example. The AI writes "train" when the student said "rain." The microphone picked up similar sound waves for "r" and "tr." Give the AI more voice examples; speak more clearly; train it on similar sounding words. Situation 1. The AI thinks a picture of a small wolf is a "dog." Situation 2. You walk behind students playing a motion-controlled game and the game thinks you are one of the players.
text.34: Chapter 3 Patterns, Pickles, and Pencils. Complete this activity before reading chapter 3. Directions: 1. Go to quickdraw.withgoogle.com and press Play. The AI will tell you what to draw and give you 20 seconds. 2. While you draw, it says its guesses out loud. 3. After 6 drawings, a yellow page shows which pictures the AI got right and wrong. 4. Write one sentence: "I think the AI guessed (or didn't guess) my drawing because it looked like blank ." The next day at school, the morning sunlight streamed across the whiteboard as Ms. Vega wrote: "Patterns and Predictions." "Today," she said, "we're going to explore how both humans and AI organize information to make sense of the world."
text.35: Niko leaned forward. "You mean like how we group animals in science?" "A lot like that," said Ms. Vega. "When we organize things by their features-like color, size, or shape-we're looking for patterns. That's something humans do all the time." Zara raised her hand, "Like when we made that bar graph in math last week? We grouped all the types of snacks people liked and saw which ones were most popular." "Perfect example," said Ms. Vega. "A bar graph is one kind of representation, or a way to show patterns in data. Today, we'll take a look at how computers make their own kinds of representations." "Will ClassMate be helping us?" Mia asked. "Of course," Ms. Vega replied. "ClassMate is always ready to help us." Representation: A way to show information-like a map, chart, or table-that highlights certain details and leaves others out Feature: A characteristic or property used to describe something (like color, size, or shape) Now, time for an experiment.
text.36: Ms. Vega walked between the tables, setting down small boxes filled with classroom objects: a red pyramid, a yellow tennis ball, a pink eraser, an orange marker, and a wooden block. Here's your challenge. You'll work with ClassMate to sort these items. Let's see how humans and computers do it differently.
text.37: She tapped her tablet, and the familiar blue swirl appeared on the board. "Remember the Object Viewer tool we used yesterday to see how ClassMate sensed items? Today, instead of asking ClassMate to just name what it sees, we'll ask it to look for patterns in the sensing data and group objects it thinks belong together." Zara's group opened the "Object Viewer" tool on their tablet. The app used the camera to scan each item in the tray and list what it detected on the screen. It's working! Niko tilted his head. "That's it?" "What do you mean?" Zara asked. "It didn't say anything about how big they are," Niko said. "Or what they're made of. Or what you actually use them for." Ms. Vega nodded. "That's an important observation. Right now, ClassMate is only paying attention to the visual features it was trained to notice, mainly shape and color."
text.38: Mia picked up the eraser and the block, one in each hand. "So it knows the eraser is a rectangular prism and the block is a cube... but it doesn't know one is soft and one is hard." "And it doesn't know that one belongs in the supply bin and the other belongs in the building center," added Niko. "Correct," said Ms. Vega. "Computers don't understand objects the way we do. They find patterns in the pixels and make a guess. Sometimes it's a good guess. Sometimes it isn't." Zara raised her hand. "But we can sort these way better. Like I know this eraser is soft and the block is hard." "Well, that's because humans use experience, memory, and context," explained Ms. Vega. "Computers only use the visual features they were trained to notice. So now it's our turn to teach ClassMate which features actually matter." Ms. Vega passed out blank feature charts with columns labeled: Object Shape Color Texture/ Size Purpose/ Use
text.39: "Before we let ClassMate try sorting your items, I want you to make a human-made representation," she said. "Describe each object using the features you think matter most." Zara filled in her chart quickly. As Mia scribbled thoughtfully, she asked Ms. Vega, Should texture count? Or size? I mean, the eraser looks like the block if you squint, but it feels different. "That's part of the challenge," Ms. Vega said as she walked past. "Humans choose which features help us solve a problem. Computers only use the features they've been trained to notice by looking at many examples and also non-examples of objects."
text.40: Example: A piece of data that shows an AI what something is, such as a drawing of a cookie Non-example: A piece of data that shows an AI what something is not, such as a drawing that looks similar but is not a cookie Niko frowned, "But how do we know what the right features are? Things can be sorted in tons of different ways." Mia nodded. "Yeah - like, we could sort by color, or by shape, or by what they're used for. How do we know which features matter?" Ms. Vega smiled. "That's the big question. Humans decide which features are important depending on the task." She glanced toward the door. "Think about Mr. Taylor in the library. When he puts books on the shelves, does he sort them by color?" No, he sorts them by topic, like Space, Mystery, or Friendship. "You're right," said Ms. Vega. "So color is a feature, but it doesn't really help you find the book you're looking for." She paused. "What do you think would happen if Mr. Taylor sorted all the library books by color instead?" Mia didn't hesitate. "It would take forever to find a book."
text.41: "And you might miss the one you actually wanted," Zara added. "Yes," said Ms. Vega. "That's why the task matters. If we choose features that don't match the goal, our sorting won't be helpful." She gestured back to the objects on the table. "When humans train AI, we decide which features matter for the task. If we choose the wrong ones, the AI can learn unhelpful patterns. That's why we test our ideas, to make sure they actually work." When all the groups finished their feature charts, Ms. Vega asked them to switch back to the tablet. "Now we'll ask ClassMate to sort your items into groups," she said. "Let's see what patterns it finds." Zara tapped SORT. Immediately, ClassMate divided the objects into three groups:
text.42: Ms. Vega raised her hand gently. "Class, let's pause for a moment," Ms. Vega said. "I want you to really think about what ClassMate just did. Its sorting might look surprising, and this is a perfect time to see how another AI makes guesses. We're going to try a tool called Quick Draw to help us understand how computers make predictions." Go to this website: quickdraw.withgoogle.com. The students typed quickly and a white screen with a yellow button appeared on their tablets. "When you click the 'Let's Draw' button at the bottom of your screen, you will hear the AI tell you something to draw. As you draw, listen carefully as Quick Draw says its guesses out loud." "Try drawing just one item," she continued. "It's okay if your drawing is messy! Computers don't care about perfect drawings. They only look for patterns."  • How does the task (what you're trying to do) change which features matter most?
text.43: The room filled with quiet scribbling and bursts of laughter as the AI voice guessed: "I see a circle... maybe it's a donut... is it a face?" Niko looked up with a laugh, "It thinks my flower is a cookie!" Ms. Vega smiled. "Quick Draw was doing what ClassMate just did. It's looking for the most obvious visual patterns and comparing them to examples it's seen before. Sometimes AI makes good guesses, and sometimes it doesn't. That's because it only looks at the features it has learned."
text.44: When each student finished, the screen shifted to a yellow results page showing which drawings the AI got right and which ones it got wrong. "Take a moment," she said, moving between the tables. "Look at one picture that the AI didn't guess correctly. Then write one short sentence: The AI got this wrong because it only looked at blank." "I think it only looked at the outline, not the details." "It's the same as how ClassMate grouped stuff by color." "It's kind of like the pencil and pickle thing again!"
text.45: What did you write? The AI got this wrong because it kept guessing the most common thing. That's an important idea. She looked up at the class. "Quick Draw learned by being trained with lots of drawings. Some of those drawings were examples of cookies, and some were not. Over time, the AI learned which drawings matched a cookie, and which ones didn't." Niko raised his hand. "So if most people draw cookies as circles, it's always going to guess 'cookie'?" "Exactly," said Ms. Vega. "And if something is less common, the computer is more likely to get it wrong." Mia frowned. "That doesn't seem fair to the drawings that are different." Ms. Vega smiled slightly. "That's something people who design AI have to think about. When one pattern shows up a lot more than others, the computer can overlook or misjudge the uncommon ones, unless humans notice and fix it."
text.46: Ms. Vega let the room settle before speaking again. "What we're seeing with these two programs," she said, "is that computers often focus on the most obvious visual patterns. For some tools, that's basic shapes. For others, color might be the strongest feature they detect." "But that's not always a useful way to sort things," Mia said. "That's true," Ms. Vega replied. "Colors or shapes might be easy for tools like ClassMate or Quick Draw to notice. But easy-to-see features aren't always the ones that help with the task you're trying to solve."
text.47: She gestured to Malik's screen. "Quick Draw isn't wrong when it guesses 'whale' instead of 'submarine.' Those shapes look similar. It just doesn't know why you're drawing it or what you plan to do with it. And ClassMate did the same thing earlier it grouped objects by features it could detect, not by how you would use them." Mia flipped back to her feature chart. "Like...when you're shopping online," she said slowly. "If I'm looking for school supplies, I want erasers and markers together. Not markers and tennis balls, even if they're the same color." Yeah. If a store sorted everything by color, it would be really annoying. It would. Color is a feature but it's not always a helpful one. So what really changed there? The task. What you're trying to do. • What happens if you leave out an important feature when sorting objects? • Can you think of a time when two things looked similar but worked very differently? • Who might be affected if an AI system chooses the wrong features?
text.48: Ms. Vega smiled. "That's it. When humans design AI systems, we decide the task first. Then we choose features that actually help with that task. If we choose the wrong features, the results won't make sense, no matter how smart the AI is." She paused, then added, "That's the key idea I want you to remember today: representations don't show everything. They focus on certain features and leave other details out. Humans decide which features matter based on the goal. Computers don't make that decision on their own. They use only the features they've been trained to notice." And that's why humans still need to be involved. We decide the purpose. We choose the features. And we check whether the results actually make sense.
text.50: Chapter 3 Activities. ACTIVITY 1 - Which feature tricked ClassMate? Directions: 1. Choose two objects that look a little bit alike. 2. Draw Object 1 and Object 2. 3. Circle one feature that made them look similar: Color / Shape / Size 4. Finish this sentence: ClassMate got confused because both objects have similar blank . ACTIVITY 2 - Make a sorting rule directions: 1. Choose two objects that look somewhat alike. 2. Come up with a rule for how an AI could sort objects (ex: "Round things go together"). 3. Write your rule. 4. Draw two things that match the rule. 5. Draw one thing that does NOT match the rule.
text.51: ACTIVITY 3 - Why did the AI get it wrong? Directions: 1. Play one round of quickdraw.withgoogle.com (6 drawings). 2. Look at the final yellow page. 3. Choose one picture the AI guessed wrong. 4. Write ONE short sentence in the space below: 5. The AI got this wrong because it only looked at blank . (shape / lines / color / number of strokes) Write your sentence here.
text.52: Chapter 4 Learning How to choose the Perfect Book. By the time the class walked into the library again, no one expected ClassMate to be perfect. Right away Zara noticed it, the small blue swirl glowing on the library checkout screen, just the same as before. But now, the students eyed it with more apprehension. "Remember last time?" Niko whispered. "When it kept giving me space books?" "Yeah," Mia said, louder. "It told me to read a book about drawing faces when I asked it for a book about friendship." Mr. Taylor, the librarian, called out from behind the desk. "Good memory, Mia" he said. "Today, you're not here to use ClassMate. You're here to understand more about how AI systems like ClassMate make decisions." He continued, "You've already seen what happens when an AI system relies on limited information. Today, we're going to design our own way of making recommendations and compare it to ClassMate's."
text.53: Zara blinked. "Wait. We get to build our own ClassMate?" "Sort of," Mr. Taylor called over his shoulder as he walked over to a cart piled high with books. "Nothing fancy. But it will help you see how decisions happen step by step." He rolled the cart to the seating area where Ms. Vega's class had gathered. It was stacked with books: mysteries, biographies, graphic novels, sports stories, science books, and poetry. "Here's the challenge," he said. "Imagine you're designing a system to help your classmates choose a book." "Sounds easy," James said. Mr. Taylor raised an eyebrow. "Does it?"
text.54: He wrote a question on the mobile whiteboard he normally kept near the circulation desk. How should AI decide which book to recommend? Hands shot up. By what they like! By what they read before. By how hard the book is. Mr. Taylor nodded. "Those are all possible criteria. But a computer can't use all of them at once unless we tell it exactly how." He added another sentence under the question: Computers make decisions by following rules humans design. He then drew a simple diagram on the board, boxes and circles connected by arrows. A decision tree: is a step-by-step set of yes-or-no questions used to sort or classify information. Each answer leads to the next question until a decision is reached A dataset: is a collection of examples used to train or test an AI system
text.55: "At each step," he explained, "the computer asks a yes-or-no question. This is called a decision tree." He wrote the first box: Does the reader like fiction? Yes. No. "Each question narrows the choices. Eventually, the computer reaches a decision." "And every question you choose affects the outcome." Mr. Taylor handed each table of students a small stack of book cards. Each card listed a library book's: Title type reading level main topic "Before you build a decision tree," he said, "you need data." Mia flipped through the cards. "So these are the examples the computer learns from?" "Yes," Mr. Taylor confirmed. "This is your dataset." Each group of students spread their cards across their table. Zara noticed something quickly. "We have a lot of mysteries." "And hardly any poetry," Malik said. "Hmm... I think that's important to note," Mr. Taylor said.
text.56: "After all, the data you choose shapes the system's decisions." Mr. Taylor looked around the tables, tapping his chin thoughtfully. "If the data shapes the decisions," he said, "then we should be able to decide how those decisions get made, right?" He flipped the whiteboard around to a clean side. "Let's try creating some rules ourselves." "Step one," Mr. Taylor said, "choose your first question." Zara's group debated. "What about 'Do you like sports?'" Niko suggested. "But that would skip over mysteries," Mia said. They settled on: The diagram asks: Does the reader want a real story? No: fiction. Yes: is the reader interested in people? Yes: biography. No: science or history.
text.57: Zara traced the arrows with her finger. "Okay... real story, yes. Interested in people, yes." "So that leads to biography," Mia said. Malik nodded. "Cool." "Okay," James said. "Now try me. I want a sports biography." The group paused. Zara traced the arrows again, slower this time. "Real story... yes. Interested in people... yes." "That still sends you to biography," Niko said. "But it doesn't say anything about sports," Mia added. "It treats all biographies the same." But I don't want any biography. We don't have a question for that. Mr. Taylor leaned over their table, "What does that tell you?" "That our rules aren't wrong," Mia said slowly. "They're just... not specific enough?" "Good thinking," Mr. Taylor said. "Your decision tree is doing what you told it to do. But when someone fits into more than one category or wants something more specific, the system can't tell the difference unless you give it another question."
text.58: Niko picked up his pencil. "So we'd need something like: 'Is the person an athlete?'" "Or 'Is sports the main topic?'" Zara added. Mr. Taylor added, "Remember, every new question you add changes what the system can and can't decide." • Which questions did the students choose first in their decision tree? • How might different questions lead to different recommendations?
text.59: They tested their decision tree with a few more readers, tracing arrows and circling boxes, until the page was crowded with pencil marks. Zara leaned back in her chair. "Okay... I think I get why ClassMate kept recommending space books before." Niko nodded. "Yeah. It wasn't trying to be annoying. It was just following the rules it had." "And probably using old data," Mia added. "'You liked space once, so you must still like space.'" Mr. Taylor smiled. "Now you're thinking like designers. When an AI system makes a decision, it's not guessing the way people do, and it doesn't have access to infinite information. It's following rules and patterns based on the data it has."
text.60: Niko kept raising questions. What if someone likes both fiction and nonfiction? What if they want something short? What if they only want books with pictures? Each question led to another arrow... and another box... and sometimes a dead end. Zara looked back over their decision tree. "Ours is doing the same thing. It's not wrong, it's just limited." As groups finished their decision trees, patterns began to emerge around the room. Mia leaned over to watch another group. "Oh," she said slowly, "Sam added a question about tone to their tree. Like serious or funny. That's a good idea." Zara flipped back through her notebook. "This is like the feature charts we made," she said. "Where we had to decide which features were most important. This is the same thing, just with questions instead of columns."
text.61: Mr. Taylor paused beside their table again. "That's a good connection, Zara" he said. "You're still choosing features. You've just turned them into decisions." Meanwhile, the decision trees themselves didn't change unless someone erased and redrew them. "It would be nice if they fixed themselves," Niko said, looking at the nub his pencil eraser had become. Mr. Taylor agreed. "When humans notice something doesn't work, we change our thinking. Computers can't do that on their own." He wrote another note on the mobile whiteboard: Humans learn flexibly. Computers learn from data and rules.
text.62: After a while, Mr. Taylor clapped loudly to get everyone's attention. "Let's pause," he said. "What did you notice while you were testing your decision trees?" "Our tree didn't work for everyone," Malik said. "Like it worked for me at first, but not James." "That's right, Malik. Now imagine it's not just James." Mr. Taylor lifted his arms to gesture all around them. "Imagine hundreds of students here at school getting recommendations they don't want. How would that affect them?" Mia immediately responded They probably wouldn't like coming to the library anymore if they kept getting recommended books they don't like. "That's why designers like you have to test the AI," Mr. Taylor said. "You have to pay attention to who is helped, who is confused, and who is left out." Mr. Taylor continued, "That's one reason AI systems struggle. They don't understand exceptions. They follow the rules they're given."
text.63: "And a lot of the time the rules only work if people fit into neat boxes," Zara added. "That's not how real people work, though," Mia said. "We change our minds. And we like more than one thing." Many students nodded their agreement. Malik raised his hand again. "Can I ask something else?" "Of course," Mr. Taylor said. "Our tree says I should read a biography," Malik said. "But... which one? There are, like, a million." Zara frowned. "Yeah. Our tree can tell the type of book, but not the exact book." "That's an important observation." Mr. Taylor agreed. "Decision trees can narrow choices, but they don't know everything. They only do what the rules allow." Mr. Taylor stepped closer to the board. "And what happens if a reader doesn't fit neatly into your questions?" James called out, "Like what if someone wants a funny true story? Or a biography that's written like a novel?" This decision tree can narrow choices, but it can't choose a specific book. What information would it need to do that?
text.64: The groups looked back at their charts. There were no paths for that. Mr. Taylor tapped the empty space at the bottom of the model diagram he had drawn. "This is where designers have to make a choice. Add another question? Collect more data? Or accept that the system has limits." Zara leaned back in her chair. "So even if the rules are logical, they don't cover everyone." "Exactly," he said. "The system isn't broken. It's doing exactly what you told it to do." Mr. Taylor glanced once more at the checkout screen, where ClassMate waited patiently. And now, you understand why tools like ClassMate need humans - not just to build them, but to test them, revise them, and decide when they aren't the best answer.
text.67: ACTIVITY- Build your own decision tree directions: Choose something you know well (sports, food, animals, games) and draw a small decision tree with at least 3 yes/no questions that leads to different answers. Example starter: "Does it live in water?"
text.68: Chapter 5 The Day We Trained a Robot. The class burst through the door after recess, cheeks flushed and voices loud. "The ball was NOT out!" Niko insisted, still holding a red rubber ball. "It totally was," Malik argued. "You stepped on the line." "I did not!" "Yes you did!" Zara dropped into her seat laughing, "We need a referee." Ms. Vega rang the bell on her desk to get the students' attention. "Okay, class - deep breath. Sounds like recess was... energetic."
text.69: "A little," Mia said, grinning. Ms. Vega reached out, and Niko handed her the ball. "So what was the problem?" "We kept switching games," Zara explained. "And every time we did, someone argued about the rules." "And everyone remembers the rules differently," Malik added. Ms. Vega paused thoughtfully. Then she smiled. "You know," she said, "this sounds like the perfect problem for a new AI helper." The chatter faded as more students turned toward her to listen.
text.70: "A new AI helper, like a robot?" Niko asked. "That's right," Ms. Vega said. "What if you had an AI helper that could recognize what game you were playing and remind everyone of the rules?" Zara's eyes lit up. "Yeah! Like a sports robot!" "That sounds like a good solution to me," Ms. Vega said. "Why don't we try it? Let's see if we can design one. What do you think?" Malik blinked. "Wait... we can create a robot?" "We can," Ms. Vega nodded. She picked up a marker and turned to the board. "Now," Ms. Vega said, "Let's go step by step, just like engineers who build AI." She began asking questions. "What is this robot designed to do?"  The students pondered how to answer the question. What if it recognizes the ball and tells you the rules? Others nodded excitedly. Chapter 5 - Activity 1: What kind of problem could a robot help solve at school or during recess? Turn to a partner and share one idea for a robot that could help solve a problem.
text.71: Ms. Vega wrote: Recognizes sports balls and explains game rules "Now," she said, "what problem does it solve?" "So people stop arguing," Zara said. The class laughed. Ms. Vega smiled. "That's part of it. But what's the bigger goal?" Malik shrugged. "So everyone follows the same rules." Mia added, "Yeah, so the game is fair." Remind me, how does a robot learn? Through data Examples And sensors, it needs a camera. Ms. Vega nodded encouragingly, "A robot helper could make sure everyone understands the rules and plays fairly. Robots learn through sensors, such as a camera, and data. We need to give it data to help it recognize different types of sports."
text.72: "What kinds of balls?" "Baseballs." "Tennis balls." "Volleyballs." "How many examples should we use?" "A lot, otherwise it'll mess up." "We could do twenty baseballs and twenty tennis balls." "Do we even have twenty volleyballs?" "Coach only has like ten." "Ten is probably fine."
text.73: Let's remember that, the amount of data used for training can affect how well AI works. Chapter 5 - Activity 2: Training data discussion if you were training a computer to recognize a ball, how many pictures would you collect? Would one picture be enough, or would you need many examples? Do all balls of the same type look the exact same? Discuss with your group why more examples might help a computer learn better.
text.74: Ms. Vega capped her marker and stepped back to look at all the notes she took. She nodded, pleased. "I think we're ready to train a robot." "But how?" Zara asked. Ms. Vega navigated to a browser window on the smartboard. A new website appeared that had big buttons, and three empty boxes labeled Class 1, Class 2, and Class 3. "We're going to use a tool that lets us train a computer model," Ms. Vega explained. "It's called Teachable Machine. Just like we talked about before, the computer will learn from examples we give it." Niko leaned forward. "So we're the trainers?" Ms. Vega nodded, "You decide what it learns." She clicked a button, and the webcam image filled the screen. Several students waved at themselves, laughing. class: in machine learning a class is a category or group that a computer learns to recognize. When you train a computer with pictures of a pencil, you're teaching it what "pencil" means - that's one class. Each class is like a labeled folder the computer sorts what it sees into
text.75: Here's your challenge. Pick three objects. Train the computer to recognize them. Then test it with something new. The room filled with the soft tapping of keys and excited chatter as everyone opened their devices. Zara's group chose a pencil, a water bottle, and an eraser. "Okay," Mia said, holding up the pencil. "Class one: pencil." They clicked Record, and the camera captured dozens of images as Mia rotated the pencil slowly. "Move it closer," Malik suggested. "Maybe different angles." Niko nodded. "And try it sideways." Across the room, someone burst out laughing. "It thinks my shoe is a sandwich!" Sam called. "That's because you only showed it one shoe," Charlotte called over her shoulder.
text.76: When Zara's group finished collecting images for all three objects, they clicked Train. A spinning circle appeared. "It's learning!" Mia said excitedly. Moments later, the model was ready. "Test time!" Niko shouted dramatically. He held up the pencil. On the screen, a green bar shot up next to the word Pencil. "Yes!" the group cheered. Malik grabbed the eraser and held it up. Another correct guess. "Okay," Zara said. "Now let's trick it."
text.77: She picked up a marker, something they hadn't trained it to recognize, and held it in front of the camera. The bars flickered wildly. Pencil — 62% Water Bottle — 21% Eraser — 17% It thinks it's a pencil! Kind of makes sense. They're both long and skinny. Ms. Vega walked over and crouched beside them. "What do you notice?" she asked. "That it guesses the closest thing," Zara said. "But it's not always right," Mia added. Ms. Vega nodded. "That's exactly how machine learning works. The computer compares what it sees to the patterns it learned from your examples." Across the room, more reactions bubbled up.
text.78: "It keeps calling everything a book!" "Oh no, mine thinks my hand is a water bottle!" "That's probably because your hand was in the pictures!" Malik suggested. Ms. Vega straightened and addressed the class. "Class, what you did today is the same process AI engineers and computer scientists use in the real world. Humans choose the data, collect the examples, test the results, and retrain when something doesn't work." She pointed toward Zara's screen.
text.79: "When your model saw the marker and guessed 'pencil,' it wasn't being silly. It was doing its best to compare what it saw with the patterns you trained it on." "Right, it just picked the closest match," Niko said. "It did," Ms. Vega agreed. "Machine learning systems don't know things the way humans do. They look for patterns in the data they were trained with." Mia tapped her notebook thoughtfully. "So if the training data is limited, the guesses will be limited too." That's the idea! More examples and more variety in the examples can help a system make better predictions.
text.80: Malik raised his hand. And if the system keeps getting something wrong, we can retrain it? "Yes," Ms. Vega said. "That's one of the most important parts of machine learning. Humans notice errors, collect better data, and train the model again." "And most importantly," Ms. Vega added, "Every step of that process depends on people. Humans decide what the system should learn, what data to collect, and how to improve it." Niko raised his hand eagerly. "So can we train one on sports balls now?" Several heads nod enthusiastically. "Oh yeah!" Zara said. "Then it can recognize what game we're playing!" "And it can tell us the rules," Malik added. Ms. Vega laughed. "It does sound like a helpful robot." "But," she continued, "we'd need a lot of training data. Baseballs, tennis balls, volleyballs, basketballs..."
text.81: "And we'd probably want pictures from lots of different angles," Mia said. "And maybe indoors and outdoors." I would think so. To train a really good model, we'd need to collect plenty of examples. Gathering all those balls and taking the pictures would take some planning. I'll need to talk with Coach White about that. I'll go get him! Ms. Vega smiled. "Not today. We have to move on to English Language Arts." A chorus of groans filled the room. "Aw man!" "But a sports robot would be so cool!" Ms. Vega tapped her chin in thought for a moment, glancing at the notes they had written earlier about their robot idea. Then a sly grin spread across her face. "Well," she said slowly, "maybe we can still work on the idea today." She turned back to the board and wrote a new title across the top in big letters: SportyBot.
text.82: The class leaned forward. "We may not be able to train SportyBot today," Ms. Vega said, "but we can start to build it with a story." "A story?" Malik asked. "For our Language Arts lesson," Ms. Vega explained. Suddenly the room buzzed with excitement. "Ohhh!" "That's actually awesome." "So we're telling a story about SportyBot?" Ms. Vega nodded. "Your job is to imagine how SportyBot would work and we'll write about it." Niko leaned back in his chair, smiling. "Okay," he said. SportyBot is definitely going to be the best referee ever.
text.84: Chapter 5 Activity.  Try training a machine directions: Go to teachablemachine.withgoogle.com and try training a model to recognize two or three objects near you. What happens when you show it something new? What happens when you give it more examples? What happened when you moved an object closer or farther away from the camera?

text.86: Chapter 6 People and Machines Learning Together. The room hummed with excitement as students pulled out their Language Arts notebooks. SportyBot was written across the board in big letters, surrounded by the notes they had made earlier. Niko leaned forward. "So... we're actually doing this?" Ms. Vega nodded affirmatively, "We are! But before we start writing, let's think about what makes a good story." She looked around the room.
text.87: Hands went up immediately. What does every good story include? Characters! A problem. And a solution. Details, so people understand what's happening. Somewhere interesting for the story to take place. "This is a great start," Ms. Vega said, nodding. "Stories need characters, a problem, a solution, and enough detail so the reader can follow along." She tapped the board. "Today, your story is also going to do something else. It's going to explain how a robot learns." Mia tilted her head thoughtfully, "So, it's like... a story and a lesson?" "Exactly," Ms. Vega said. "And you already have everything you need."
text.88: She gestured to the board. The notes they had created earlier were still there: ideas about sensors, data, mistakes, and how to improve the robot. Your job is to turn these ideas into a story. Zara leaned forward, studying the board. "So, the characters could be kids like us." "And the problem is arguing about the rules," Malik added. "And the solution is SportyBot," Niko said. Ms. Vega nodded. "That sounds like a strong beginning. Let's try telling the story together first, and then you can write your own versions." She stepped aside and motioned for someone to begin.
text.89: Zara raised her hand. "Okay... Once there was a group of neighborhood kids who loved playing games after school." Niko jumped in. "But every time they tried to play, they started arguing." "Like whether the ball was out," Malik added. "Or what the rules even were," Mia said. Ms. Vega smiled. "Good. That's your problem." Zara continued, "So the kids decided to build a robot to help them." "What should we call it?" Niko asked, even though the answer was obvious. The class laughed. "SportyBot!" "Okay," Zara said, writing in her notebook as she spoke. "They built SportyBot to help them play fair."
text.90: Mia leaned forward. "We should explain what it does." "It recognizes what game they're playing," Malik said. "And tells them the rules," Niko added. Ms. Vega nodded. "How does it do that?" Zara glanced at the board. "It has a camera— a vision sensor." "So, when the kids were ready to play a new game," Mia said, "they held up the ball to SportyBot." "And SportyBot used its camera to identify the ball," Malik said. "And then explain the rules of the game," Niko finished. "Great," Ms. Vega said. "Now your reader understands how people interact with the robot." Zara kept writing. "But robots don't just know everything. The kids had to train it."
text.91: Mia pointed to the board. "They showed it lots of examples." "Baseballs," Malik said. "Tennis balls," Niko added. "Volleyballs," Zara said. "How many?" Ms. Vega prompted. "Twenty baseballs," Mia said. "Twenty tennis balls," Malik added. "And only ten volleyballs," Zara said. "Because that's all they had." Niko laughed. "Coach never has enough volleyballs." Zara wrote quickly. "SportyBot learned by looking at pictures of the balls and finding patterns." Ms. Vega nodded. "Now your reader knows how the robot was trained." "Ooh-but something should go wrong!" Malik said. Ms. Vega nodded thoughtfully. "That's true for stories, and for machine learning." "In a story," she continued, "a problem in the middle makes things interesting, right? It gives the characters something to figure out."
text.92: She tapped the board lightly. "And in machine learning, systems don't usually work perfectly the first time." She glanced around the room. "Remember how many issues ClassMate had?" Malik, "How could I forget? It called me 'Mallet'!" "And made wrong book recommendations," Zara added. "Yes," Ms. Vega laughed, "But each of those mistakes showed us something the system needed to improve." Mia agreed. "My dad always says mistakes are part of learning." "That's true," Ms. Vega said. "Without errors, we wouldn't know how to make a system better." Niko grinned. "So, our story needs a mistake... and the robot needs one too." Ms. Vega clapped, "Now you're thinking like both a writer and an engineer."

"Maybe it confuses the volleyball with something else." "Like a tennis ball," Malik said. "No, a baseball!" Niko added. "Because baseballs and volleyballs are both white and round." Zara nodded, still writing. "So, the kids hold up a volleyball... and SportyBot gives them the rules for baseball." "That would be so confusing," Mia said. "Everyone would be like, 'Why are we running bases?'" Niko joked. "And trying to spike a baseball would really hurt!" James added. The class laughed again.

"Or maybe the pictures all looked the same," Mia added. Yeah, like they were all the same angle and background. "So, it didn't learn enough patterns," Niko concluded. Ms. Vega smiled. "That sounds like a very likely thing that could happen." Zara added another sentence. "The kids realized the robot needed better training." "How do they fix it?" Ms. Vega asked.
